prompt: A path is written as /home/asha/notes.txt. Does its meaning depend on where you are?
optionA: Yes; every path is read from the current directory
optionB: No; it begins at the top of the tree and means the same everywhere
optionC: Yes, unless the current directory is the top of the tree
optionD: It depends on whether the file exists
correctAnswerText: No; it begins at the top of the tree and means the same everywhere
explanation: Starting at the top fixes the meaning completely. Where the reader happens to be changes nothing about where it points.

prompt: A path is written as reports/june.txt. Does its meaning depend on where you are?
optionA: No; it names one file wherever it is used
optionB: No, because it contains a directory name
optionC: Only if the file does not exist
optionD: Yes; it is read from wherever you currently are
correctAnswerText: Yes; it is read from wherever you currently are
explanation: Not starting at the top means starting from here, and here changes. The same path reaches different files from different places.

prompt: Which of these paths means the same thing from every directory?
optionA: /var/log/system.log
optionB: log/system.log
optionC: ../log/system.log
optionD: ./system.log
correctAnswerText: /var/log/system.log
explanation: Only the first begins at the top. The other three all start from wherever the reader is.

prompt: What distinguishes the two kinds of path?
optionA: How many directory names it contains
optionB: Whether the file it names exists
optionC: Whether it starts at the top of the tree or from where you are
optionD: Whether it ends in a file name or a directory name
correctAnswerText: Whether it starts at the top of the tree or from where you are
explanation: Length and existence have nothing to do with it. A one-segment path can start at the top and a five-segment one need not.

prompt: A student says a long path must start at the top of the tree because it is detailed. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; long paths always start at the top
optionB: Length says nothing about it; a long path can still be read from where you are
optionC: Long paths are always read from where you are
optionD: The rule holds for paths of more than three segments
correctAnswerText: Length says nothing about it; a long path can still be read from where you are
explanation: A path like a/b/c/d/e/f.txt is six segments and entirely relative. Only how it begins settles the question.

prompt: A user wants to see what is inside a file. Which permission does that need?
optionA: Write
optionB: Execute
optionC: All three
optionD: Read
correctAnswerText: Read
explanation: Reading the contents needs the read permission and nothing else. The other two govern different actions entirely.

prompt: A user has write permission on a file and not read permission. What can they do?
optionA: Change the contents without being able to see them
optionB: Both change and see the contents, since write includes read
optionC: Neither, since write is useless without read
optionD: See the contents but not change them
correctAnswerText: Change the contents without being able to see them
explanation: The three are independent rather than ranked, so having one grants nothing about the others. Writing without reading is unusual and entirely possible.

prompt: Which statement about the three permissions is true?
optionA: Write implies read, since changing needs seeing
optionB: Execute implies read and write
optionC: Each is granted separately and none implies another
optionD: They form a ladder, with each including the ones below
correctAnswerText: Each is granted separately and none implies another
explanation: Independence is the whole design. The ladder reading is intuitive and makes every real access question come out wrong.

prompt: A student cannot run a script and says it must be because they lack read permission on it. The read permission is granted and the execute permission is not. What is the actual obstacle?
optionA: The missing read permission, which running also requires
optionB: The missing execute permission, which is what running requires
optionC: Both permissions are needed and both are missing
optionD: Nothing; the script should run
correctAnswerText: The missing execute permission, which is what running requires
explanation: Running needs execute, and read is separately granted here. Assuming one permission covers another is what produces this diagnosis.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha. Asha opens it. Which set of permissions applies to her?
optionA: The group set
optionB: The everyone-else set
optionC: Whichever of the three is most generous
optionD: The owner set
correctAnswerText: The owner set
explanation: She is the owner, so the owner set governs. The other two describe other people.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha and belongs to the group "editors". Ravi is in that group and is not the owner. Which set applies to Ravi?
optionA: The group set
optionB: The owner set
optionC: The everyone-else set
optionD: The owner set and the group set together
correctAnswerText: The group set
explanation: Ravi falls into the group class, so that set governs him. He is judged by one set rather than a combination.

prompt: How many of the three sets apply to any one user?
optionA: All three
optionB: One or two, depending on the file
optionC: Exactly one
optionD: Whichever ones grant the action being attempted
correctAnswerText: Exactly one
explanation: A user falls into the first class that describes them and is judged by that set alone. Combining the sets is not how the decision is made.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha, whose owner set grants read only. It belongs to a group Asha is in, whose group set grants read and write. Can Asha write to the file?
optionA: Yes; the group set grants write and she is in the group
optionB: No; she is the owner, so the owner set governs and it grants no write
optionC: Yes; the most generous applicable set applies
optionD: It cannot be determined without the everyone-else set
correctAnswerText: No; she is the owner, so the owner set governs and it grants no write
explanation: Being the owner is what decides which set is consulted, and it is not the most generous one here. This surprises almost everyone the first time they meet it.

prompt: The current directory is /home/asha. A path is written as reports/june.txt. Which file does it reach?
optionA: /reports/june.txt
optionB: /home/reports/june.txt
optionC: /home/asha/june.txt
optionD: /home/asha/reports/june.txt
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/reports/june.txt
explanation: The relative path is joined to the current directory. Reading it from the top instead gives the first wrong answer.

prompt: The current directory is /var/www/site/public. A path is written as assets/img/logo.png. Which file does it reach?
optionA: /var/www/site/public/assets/img/logo.png
optionB: /assets/img/logo.png
optionC: /var/www/site/assets/img/logo.png
optionD: /var/www/site/public/img/logo.png
correctAnswerText: /var/www/site/public/assets/img/logo.png
explanation: Every segment of the relative path is appended to the current directory in order. Dropping one level or one segment produces the other answers.

prompt: A developer sitting in /home/asha/reports types a path made of two dots, a slash, and then notes.txt. Where does that land?
optionA: /home/asha/reports/notes.txt
optionB: /home/notes.txt
optionC: /home/asha/notes.txt
optionD: /notes.txt
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/notes.txt
explanation: Two dots mean the directory above, which from reports is asha, and notes.txt is taken from there. A second climb would have reached /home.

prompt: A build script runs from /a/b/c/d and refers to ../../x/y.txt. How many levels does it climb, and where does it end up?
optionA: One level, ending at /a/b/c/x/y.txt
optionB: Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt
optionC: Three levels, ending at /a/x/y.txt
optionD: Two levels, ending at /a/x/y.txt
correctAnswerText: Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt
explanation: Each pair of dots climbs once, so two pairs climb from d to b, giving Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt. Miscounting the climbs is what produces the other three.

prompt: A file grants its owner read and write, its group read only, and everyone else nothing. Ravi is in the group and wants to read it. Is he allowed?
optionA: No; only the owner may read it
optionB: Yes; he may read and write it
optionC: It cannot be determined without knowing the owner
optionD: Yes; the group set grants read
correctAnswerText: Yes; the group set grants read
explanation: Ravi falls in the group class and that set grants read. It does not grant write, so that is where his permissions stop.

prompt: Priya neither owns a document nor belongs to its group, and the everyone-else set on it permits reading and nothing more. She tries to save a change to it. What happens?
optionA: The save is refused, since the class she falls into grants no write
optionB: The save succeeds, because two of the three sets do permit writing
optionC: The save succeeds, because being able to read a file means being able to save it
optionD: The outcome depends on who else is in the group
correctAnswerText: The save is refused, since the class she falls into grants no write
explanation: She is judged by the everyone-else class alone, and it stops at reading. What the owner and group are permitted has no bearing on her.

prompt: A file grants its owner execute only, its group read and write, and everyone else read. Asha owns it and is also a member of the group. She wants to read it. A user is judged by the first class they fall into, and Asha is the owner. Is she allowed?
optionA: Yes; her group membership grants read
optionB: Yes; the everyone-else set grants read and she is a person like any other
optionC: No; the owner set grants execute only
optionD: Yes; owners may always read their own files
correctAnswerText: No; the owner set grants execute only
explanation: The owner class is consulted and it grants no read, so the more generous sets never come into it. Owning a file does not carry any permission of its own.

prompt: What does read permission on a directory allow?
optionA: Reading the contents of the files inside it
optionB: Seeing the names of what is inside it
optionC: Reaching a file inside it whose name you know
optionD: Adding a file to it
correctAnswerText: Seeing the names of what is inside it
explanation: A directory holds names, so reading it lists names. What those files contain is governed by their own permissions.

prompt: A directory grants execute and not read. A user knows the exact name of a file inside it. What can they do?
optionA: Nothing, since they cannot read the directory
optionB: List the contents but not reach any file
optionC: Both list the contents and reach the file
optionD: Reach that file by name, without being able to list what else is there
correctAnswerText: Reach that file by name, without being able to list what else is there
explanation: Execute on a directory permits passing through to something named. Read permits listing, and the two are separate.

prompt: A directory grants read and not execute. A user wants to open a file inside it. Reading the directory lists the names, and reaching anything inside requires execute, which is not granted. What happens?
optionA: They can see the file name and cannot open it
optionB: They can open the file, since they can see it
optionC: They can neither see nor open it
optionD: They can open it but not see it listed
correctAnswerText: They can see the file name and cannot open it
explanation: Being able to see a name is not being able to reach what it names. This combination produces the confusing result of a visible file that cannot be opened.

prompt: Removing a file changes which thing?
optionA: The file itself
optionB: Both the file and the directory equally
optionC: The directory that lists it
optionD: Neither; removal is handled separately
correctAnswerText: The directory that lists it
explanation: The name is an entry in the directory, and removing the file removes that entry. That is why the directory permissions are what govern it.

prompt: A file grants nobody write permission. Its directory grants write to everyone. Can an ordinary user remove the file?
optionA: No; the file grants no write permission
optionB: Yes; removal is governed by the directory, which grants write
optionC: No; both the file and the directory must grant write
optionD: Only the owner of the file may remove it
correctAnswerText: Yes; removal is governed by the directory, which grants write
explanation: The file own permissions govern changing its contents rather than its existence. A read-only file in a writable directory can be removed by anyone who can write to that directory.

prompt: A team protects an important file by removing every write permission from it. It sits in a directory that grants write to everyone. Removing a file changes the directory that lists it, and the directory grants write to everyone. Is the file protected from deletion?
optionA: Yes; a file with no write permission cannot be removed
optionB: Yes, unless the user owns the file
optionC: It depends on whether the file is currently open
optionD: No; anyone who can write to the directory can still remove it
correctAnswerText: No; anyone who can write to the directory can still remove it
explanation: The protection guards the contents and not the existence. Removing write from the directory is what would actually prevent deletion.

prompt: A summary reads rw-r--r--, in the order owner, group, everyone else, with each group of three in the order read, write, execute. What may the owner do?
optionA: Read and write, but not execute
optionB: Read only
optionC: Read, write and execute
optionD: Write only
correctAnswerText: Read and write, but not execute
explanation: The first group of three is rw-, which grants read and write with execute absent. The dash marks a permission that is not granted.

prompt: Two files are compared. One carries the summary r-xr-x--- and the other rwxr-x---. Groups of three run owner, then group, then everyone else; within each group the order is read, write, execute. What is the only difference between them?
optionA: The group may write on the second and not on the first
optionB: Everyone else gains read on the second
optionC: The owner may write on the second and not on the first
optionD: There is no difference between the two
correctAnswerText: The owner may write on the second and not on the first
explanation: Only the second character differs, and it sits in the owner group at the write position. The remaining six characters are identical.

prompt: A summary reads ---rwxrwx, in the order owner, group, everyone else, with each group in the order read, write, execute. The owner asks why they cannot open the file. The first group of three describes the owner and it grants nothing. What is the position?
optionA: The owner has full access, since owners always do
optionB: The owner is granted nothing, while everyone else has full access
optionC: The summary is invalid, since an owner cannot have fewer permissions than others
optionD: The owner may read but not write
correctAnswerText: The owner is granted nothing, while everyone else has full access
explanation: The arrangement is unusual and entirely legal, and the owner is judged by their own group of three. Owning the file carries no permission by itself.

prompt: The current directory is /home/asha. Do the paths notes.txt and /home/asha/notes.txt reach the same file?
optionA: No; they are written differently
optionB: No; one is relative and one is absolute
optionC: Only if the file exists
optionD: Yes; the relative one resolves to the absolute one from here
correctAnswerText: Yes; the relative one resolves to the absolute one from here
explanation: Resolving the relative path from the stated directory gives exactly the absolute one. Looking different is not being different.

prompt: The current directory is /a/b. Do the paths ../b/c.txt and c.txt reach the same file?
optionA: Yes; going up to /a and back into b returns to where you started
optionB: No; the first goes up a level and the second does not
optionC: No; the first names b explicitly
optionD: Only if /a/b contains a directory called b
correctAnswerText: Yes; going up to /a and back into b returns to where you started
explanation: Up one level and back down into the same directory is a round trip. Both paths resolve to /a/b/c.txt.

prompt: A script uses the path data/input.csv and works when run from /home/asha/project. A colleague runs the same script from /home/asha and it fails. The path is relative and is resolved from whichever directory the script is run from. Which file was it looking for the second time?
optionA: /home/asha/project/data/input.csv
optionB: /data/input.csv
optionC: /home/asha/data/input.csv
optionD: /home/asha/project/input.csv
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/data/input.csv
explanation: The relative path was joined to the second directory rather than the first. Nothing moved and nothing about the script changed.

prompt: A user cannot open /projects/secret/plan.txt. The file grants read to everyone. The directory /projects/secret grants the user nothing. What is blocking them?
optionA: The file, which must be misconfigured
optionB: The directory on the way, which they cannot pass through
optionC: The top of the tree, which is restricted
optionD: Nothing; the file should open
correctAnswerText: The directory on the way, which they cannot pass through
explanation: Reaching a file requires passing through every directory on the way to it. A perfectly readable file inside an unreachable directory cannot be opened.

prompt: A user cannot open /var/data/reports/q1.txt. Every directory on the path grants them execute, and the file grants read to its owner and to nobody else. The user is not the owner and is not in the group. Every directory on the path is passable and the file grants read only to its owner. What is blocking them?
optionA: A directory on the path, which they cannot pass through
optionB: The group, which they are not a member of
optionC: Nothing; the file should open
optionD: The file itself, since the class they fall into is granted no read
correctAnswerText: The file itself, since the class they fall into is granted no read
explanation: The path is clear all the way, which rules out the directories. Not being in the group is why they fall into the everyone-else class rather than being the obstacle itself.

prompt: A command using the path config/settings.json worked yesterday from one directory and fails today. The file is still present and still readable when reached by its full path from the top. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The command was run from a different directory, so the relative path resolved elsewhere
optionB: The file was moved
optionC: The file permissions were changed
optionD: The file was deleted and recreated
correctAnswerText: The command was run from a different directory, so the relative path resolved elsewhere
explanation: The file being reachable by its full path rules out both moving and permissions. What changed is where the relative path was resolved from.

prompt: A scheduled job using a relative path succeeds when a developer runs it by hand and fails when the scheduler runs it. The file is present and readable by the account the scheduler uses. The file is readable by the scheduler account and the path is relative. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The scheduler account lacks permission on the file
optionB: The scheduler runs the job at a time when the file is absent
optionC: The scheduler starts the job in a different directory from the one the developer runs it in
optionD: The relative path is malformed
correctAnswerText: The scheduler starts the job in a different directory from the one the developer runs it in
explanation: Permissions are stated to be in order, which leaves where the job starts. Schedulers commonly start jobs somewhere quite unlike a developer session.

prompt: A file grants read to its owner only. Read is added to the everyone-else set so that one colleague can see it. Who gains access?
optionA: Only that colleague
optionB: Everyone on the system, not only that colleague
optionC: Only members of the file group
optionD: Nobody, until the colleague is added to the group
correctAnswerText: Everyone on the system, not only that colleague
explanation: The everyone-else set describes everyone outside the owner and the group. Adding the colleague to the group and granting the group instead is the narrower change.

prompt: A directory is granted write for everyone so that a team can add files to it. The directory already contains files belonging to several people. Write on a directory permits adding and removing entries, and the directory holds other people files. What else does the change permit?
optionA: Nothing else; only adding files is permitted
optionB: Anyone can now change the contents of the files in it
optionC: Anyone can now read the files in it
optionD: Anyone can now remove the files already in it, whoever owns them
correctAnswerText: Anyone can now remove the files already in it, whoever owns them
explanation: Adding and removing are the same permission on a directory. The contents of the existing files are still governed by their own permissions, which is why removal rather than modification is the exposure.

prompt: A team grants read to everyone on a directory so that a listing works, and is satisfied that the files inside remain private because their own permissions were not changed. Reading a directory lists the names inside it, and the names themselves may be revealing. What has been exposed?
optionA: The file names, which may disclose more than the team intended
optionB: Nothing; the file contents are still protected
optionC: The file contents, since directory read implies file read
optionD: Nothing, since a listing is not access
correctAnswerText: The file names, which may disclose more than the team intended
explanation: The contents really are still protected and names are information in their own right. A directory of files named after clients or incidents discloses a great deal before anything is opened.

prompt: An administrator removes execute from a directory to stop people reaching a file inside it. A colleague points out that the file is also reachable through a second directory that still grants execute. Reaching a file requires passing through the directories on the route taken, and a second route is still open. What follows?
optionA: The file is now unreachable, since one route is blocked
optionB: The change has no effect at all on either route
optionC: The file is still reachable by the other route, so the change achieved little
optionD: The second route will stop working automatically
correctAnswerText: The file is still reachable by the other route, so the change achieved little
explanation: Permissions apply along the route actually taken rather than to the file globally. Every route has to be considered, which is why access questions get harder as trees get linked.

prompt: A team removes write permission from a configuration file so that a running service cannot change it. The service runs as an account that owns the file. An owner may restore write permission on a file they own, and the service account owns this one. Does the change prevent the service from writing?
optionA: Yes; without write permission the service cannot write
optionB: No; the owner can grant write back to itself before writing
optionC: Yes, unless the service runs with administrative rights
optionD: No, because permissions do not apply to running services
correctAnswerText: No; the owner can grant write back to itself before writing
explanation: Ownership carries the ability to change permissions, which makes removing one from an owner a speed bump rather than a barrier. Changing the owner is what would actually prevent it.

prompt: A log file must be readable by a monitoring account and by nobody else, and writable by the service that produces it. The service owns the file and the monitoring account can be placed in a group. Only two parties need access and one of them owns the file. What is the narrowest arrangement?
optionA: Read and write for everyone, since only two parties will use it
optionB: Read for everyone and write for the owner
optionC: Read and write for the owner and for the group
optionD: Write for the owner, read for a group containing the monitoring account, nothing for everyone else
correctAnswerText: Write for the owner, read for a group containing the monitoring account, nothing for everyone else
explanation: Each party gets exactly what it needs and nobody else gets anything. Granting the group write or everyone read both hand out access nobody asked for.

prompt: A shared directory must let team members add their own files and must stop them removing one another files. Write on a directory permits both adding and removing, and the two cannot be separated by the three ordinary permissions. What follows?
optionA: The ordinary three permissions cannot express this, so an additional mechanism is needed
optionB: Grant write to the group, which permits adding only
optionC: Grant write to the owner only, and let others add through the group
optionD: Remove write from the directory and grant it on each file
correctAnswerText: The ordinary three permissions cannot express this, so an additional mechanism is needed
explanation: Adding and removing are one permission, so no arrangement of the three achieves the split. Systems provide an extra directory setting for exactly this case, and recognising that the basic three cannot do it is the step that matters.

prompt: A script must be runnable by a group and must not be readable by them, so that the group cannot see how it works. Running a script requires the system to read its text, so execute without read does not work for a script. What follows?
optionA: Grant execute without read, which achieves exactly this
optionB: Grant read without execute, and run it another way
optionC: The requirement cannot be met for a script, since running it requires reading it
optionD: Grant both and rely on the group not to look
correctAnswerText: The requirement cannot be met for a script, since running it requires reading it
explanation: A compiled program can be executed without being readable, and a script cannot, because the interpreter has to read the text. The distinction is what makes this requirement impossible as stated.

prompt: A team can grant read to everyone on a directory of documentation, or maintain a group containing every person who needs it. The documentation is public information and the group would need updating every time somebody joins or leaves. The content is public and the group requires ongoing maintenance. Which fits?
optionA: Maintain the group, since narrow permissions are always preferable
optionB: Grant read to everyone, since the content is public and the group buys nothing
optionC: Maintain the group, since it records who has access
optionD: Grant read to everyone and also maintain the group
correctAnswerText: Grant read to everyone, since the content is public and the group buys nothing
explanation: Narrowing is worth paying for when there is something to protect, and here there is not. The group would be maintenance in exchange for restricting access to information that is not restricted.

prompt: An engineer is repeatedly blocked by permissions and proposes granting themselves full access to everything to save time. The permissions currently prevent a mistake in one area from affecting the others, and full access would remove that separation everywhere. What is the trade?
optionA: Nothing; full access is obviously correct for an engineer
optionB: Nothing; full access is obviously wrong in every case
optionC: Whether the engineer is trusted by their colleagues
optionD: Time saved against losing the containment that stops one mistake spreading
correctAnswerText: Time saved against losing the containment that stops one mistake spreading
explanation: The question is not about trust, since a trusted person makes mistakes too. What permissions buy here is that an error in one area stays there.

prompt: A document system records, for each document, an owner, a team, and a default for everyone else, with view and edit granted separately. A document grants its owner view only, its team view and edit, and everyone else view. The owner is also on the team. The owner class is consulted first and it grants view only. Can the owner edit it?
optionA: No; the owner class grants view only
optionB: Yes; their team membership grants edit
optionC: Yes; owners can always edit their own documents
optionD: It cannot be determined from the description
correctAnswerText: No; the owner class grants view only
explanation: The described system is the file permission model under other names, and the same conclusion follows. Being consulted first is what makes the owner class binding rather than a floor.

prompt: A storage service grants list and read as separate permissions on a container. A team grants read and not list, and a user complains they cannot find anything. Read permits fetching an item whose name is known, and list permits discovering the names. What can the user do?
optionA: Nothing, since they cannot see what is there
optionB: List the contents but not fetch anything
optionC: Fetch any item whose name they already know, without being able to discover names
optionD: Both list and fetch, since read implies list
correctAnswerText: Fetch any item whose name they already know, without being able to discover names
explanation: This is directory execute and directory read under other names. The combination is deliberate in storage services, where names are often known in advance.

prompt: A repository grants a user write on a folder of files. A colleague argues this means the user can also delete the folder itself. Write on the folder governs what happens inside it, while removing the folder changes the thing that contains it. Is the colleague right?
optionA: Yes; write on a folder includes removing it
optionB: No; removing the folder is governed by whatever contains the folder
optionC: Yes, if the user also owns the folder
optionD: It cannot be determined without knowing the repository
correctAnswerText: No; removing the folder is governed by whatever contains the folder
explanation: The same reasoning that puts file deletion under the directory puts folder deletion under the parent. Permission on a thing governs what happens inside it rather than its own existence.

prompt: A team must decide whether to grant access to a shared area by adding each person individually or by maintaining one group. People join and leave every month, and the same access is needed on forty separate areas. Individual grants would have to be made and removed on forty areas for every joiner and leaver. Which fits?
optionA: Individual grants, since they are more precise
optionB: Individual grants, since groups grant more than is needed
optionC: Either, since the resulting access is identical
optionD: The group, since membership is changed once rather than forty times per person
correctAnswerText: The group, since membership is changed once rather than forty times per person
explanation: The resulting access is identical, which is why correctness cannot decide it. What decides it is that one change to a group is forty changes avoided, and forty places to forget is forty places someone keeps access they should have lost.
